video_title: Midterm Tsunami, Equity Perps + Uncensored Ai - The Chopping Block
gist: The Chopping Block hosts dissect the Democratic midterm 'mega tsunami': prediction markets (Polymarket 419/426) beat polls, crypto legislation is likely frozen for two years despite a two-to-one pro-crypto Congress, and anti-data-center politics is reshaping AI compute economics (bullish incumbents/hyperscalers, bearish neoclouds/chips, accelerating non-US build-out). They also cover the CFTC clearing US equity perps (sued by Cboe and Citadel) and defend abliterated uncensored AI models against FAI's regulation push.

themes.theme: Prediction markets vs polls in the midterm blue tsunami

insights.claim: Polymarket reported that the favorite won in 419 of 426 US midterm races, and by about 7pm on election night it priced ~99% that Democrats would take total control of Congress.
insights.speaker: Haseeb (Dragonfly)
insights.so_what: Strong calibration evidence for prediction markets as a real-time election information source, supporting the category (Dragonfly is an investor).
insights.quote: Polymarket published that uh 419 of 426 races, the favorite on Polymarket ended up winning.

insights.claim: Prediction markets priced a clean Democratic sweep at roughly 80% (high 70s) for about a week and a half before the midterms, while mainstream outlets like the NYT and WSJ lagged.
insights.speaker: Haseeb (Dragonfly)
insights.so_what: Markets led mainstream media by days to hours in resolving the election outcome.
insights.quote: It was 80% clean clean sweep for like a week and a half before.

insights.claim: Polls underweighted Democrats rather than overweighting them; prediction markets were accurate in aggregate only because the polling error happened to point in the direction markets already leaned, so markets still underpriced the true magnitude of the wave.
insights.speaker: Robert (Superstate)
insights.so_what: Prediction-market accuracy was partly luck in error direction; individual deep-red races were systematically mispriced.
insights.quote: I also think the prediction markets underpriced the true odds in that case because they were quite well aligned with the polls.

insights.claim: At the race-level microstructure, prediction markets badly mispriced deep-red contests, e.g. the Mississippi Senate race traded around 7% for Democrats before resolving to 100%, decided by roughly a 50-vote margin.
insights.speaker: Robert / Tarun
insights.so_what: Aggregate national markets are well calibrated, but tail single-race markets in wave years offer mispricing opportunities.
insights.quote: Mississippi was at like, you know, 7%, right? Before going to 100%

insights.claim: Prediction markets and Brazilian public markets strongly priced a Bolsonaro win in the recent Brazilian election, but Lula won by about 3%, a large miss also visible in Brazilian stocks and banks trading.
insights.speaker: Tom
insights.so_what: Prediction markets are less reliable in lower-liquidity foreign elections; a cautionary counterexample.

insights.claim: After the midterms, prediction markets priced a 68% chance that a Democrat wins in 2028, with Jon Ossoff now the single most likely candidate ahead of AOC and Gavin Newsom, and JD Vance still the Republican frontrunner with Rubio a few points behind.
insights.speaker: Haseeb (Dragonfly)
insights.so_what: 2028 base case now tilts Democratic; crypto policy after 2028 hinges on a candidate whose views are less known.
insights.quote: it's now pricing 68% chance that the 2028 victor will be Democrat.

themes.theme: Crypto policy under a Democratic Congress

insights.claim: Stand With Crypto ratings show the incoming House at 226 pro-crypto vs 106 anti-crypto members and the Senate cohort at 19 pro-crypto vs 8 anti-crypto, roughly a two-to-one pro-crypto margin despite the Democratic wave.
insights.speaker: Haseeb (Dragonfly)
insights.so_what: The structural composition of Congress remains crypto-friendly even as party control flips.
insights.quote: 226 pro-crypto candidates came into the House, 106 anti-crypto.

insights.claim: Because the blue wave reached deep-red districts where Democrats ran centrist candidates, many newly elected members are moderate and pro-crypto (e.g. Talarico, a Bitcoin-friendly Texan who voted on the Texas Bitcoin reserve), so there are fewer far-left seats than the headline suggests.
insights.speaker: Robert (Superstate)
insights.so_what: Post-Trump Congress may be pragmatic on crypto once the corruption theme fades.
insights.quote: There's a lot of moderates who've come in.

insights.claim: Sherrod Brown, a well-known crypto industry opponent, won his race despite Fairshake PAC spending around $40 million to defeat him.
insights.speaker: Haseeb (Dragonfly)
insights.so_what: Crypto PAC money failed to stop a key adversary; a prominent crypto critic returns to the Senate.
insights.quote: in this cycle it was like 40 million.

insights.claim: The next two years in Washington will be dominated by Trump corruption themes, including World Liberty Financial and the Trump meme coin, which will be repeatedly aired in hearings and on TV.
insights.speaker: Haseeb (Dragonfly)
insights.so_what: Crypto is reputationally tied to Trump corruption narratives through 2028, a headwind for the industry's image.
insights.quote: it's very clear next 2 years the main theme is going to be Trump corruption, World Liberty Financial, Trump Coin

insights.claim: The chance of any crypto legislation, including the Clarity Act, becoming law in the next two years is basically zero: Democrats will posture and Trump will veto, so crypto policy in DC goes quiet.
insights.speaker: Robert (Superstate)
insights.so_what: Do not underwrite investments on US market-structure legislation passing before 2029.
insights.quote: I think the chances that we get any legislation basically zero.

insights.claim: Maxine Waters is already floating draft text for a revamped crypto market-structure bill that could return framed as an AML bill, while Elizabeth Warren wants a bill that regulates crypto into obsolescence.
insights.speaker: Robert (Superstate)
insights.so_what: Any future bill will likely carry heavier AML and ethics provisions than the prior Clarity Act draft.

insights.claim: There is a minority possibility that Trump, like Clinton and Obama after midterm losses, pivots hard toward bipartisanship, potentially accepting ethics provisions in a crypto bill; the other hosts consider this unlikely.
insights.speaker: Robert (Superstate)
insights.so_what: A tail scenario in which crypto legislation unexpectedly passes with ethics provisions.
insights.quote: There's a chance that Trump pivots hard and says, "You know what? Sure, ethics provisions in the crypto bill. Let's do it."

insights.claim: Trump has not made America the crypto capital of the world, and launching the Trump meme coin damaged the industry's political prospects; corruption was a leading issue in exit polls.
insights.speaker: Robert / Tarun
insights.so_what: Crypto's alignment with Trump became a political liability.
insights.quote: I think that Trump the meme coins basically

insights.claim: Every Democratic senator voted against the Clarity Act, while Ossoff voted for the GENIUS stablecoin bill, and for Ossoff the bigger policy issue is likely data centers given Georgia build-outs rather than crypto.
insights.speaker: Tarun / Robert
insights.so_what: Stablecoins retain bipartisan support even as broader market-structure legislation is partisan.
insights.quote: Every single Democratic senator voted against clarity.

themes.theme: CFTC equity perps and incumbent pushback

insights.claim: On midterm day CFTC chairman Mike Cilec (as transcribed) cleared single-stock perpetual futures to trade in the US on DCMs that are SEC notice-registered for security futures, explicitly to onshore activity from offshore unregulated venues.
insights.speaker: Haseeb (Dragonfly)
insights.so_what: A major regulatory unlock that lets equity perps trade onshore in the US.
insights.quote: single stock perps can now trade on DCMs that are SEC notice registered for security futures.

insights.claim: Within hours of the CFTC equity-perps clearance, Cboe and Citadel sued, arguing the products are swaps that should be restricted.
insights.speaker: Haseeb (Dragonfly)
insights.so_what: Litigation risk could delay the launch of US equity perps.
insights.quote: Within hours, Cboe and Citadel sued.

insights.claim: Hyperliquid, through its recent partnership with ICE, is seen as a potential beneficiary of the CFTC ruling allowing equity perps onshore.
insights.speaker: Haseeb (Dragonfly)
insights.so_what: Hyperliquid may gain a regulated US distribution path for equity perps.

insights.claim: Citadel Securities' opposition to equity perps is puzzling because, as a market maker, a new market is free volume; one possible reason is that differing rebates on stock vs commodity exchanges plus funding rates make the single-stock perp-vs-spot arb less profitable for them.
insights.speaker: Tarun (Gauntlet)
insights.so_what: The incumbents' motives may be fee-structure economics rather than investor protection.
insights.quote: rebates on stock trade on exchanges, stock trading exchanges, and rebates on commodity exchanges are different.

insights.claim: Market makers who trade on Hyperliquid say they would move their Hyperliquid volume to the US if onshore equity perps go live, since US firms currently need awkward multi-entity setups to trade offshore.
insights.speaker: Tarun (Gauntlet)
insights.so_what: Onshore equity perps could pull market-maker liquidity from offshore venues, including Hyperliquid itself.
insights.quote: We'll move all our hyper liquid volume to the US if you do this this happens

insights.claim: Cboe and Citadel are likely suing mainly to slow the rollout and buy time to catch up and prepare, not because they oppose participating.
insights.speaker: Robert (Superstate)
insights.so_what: Expect incumbent delay tactics, not permanent blockage, of US equity perps.
insights.quote: They would all love to participate.

insights.claim: Cboe's existing single-name US equity futures (e.g. on Costco and McDonald's) trade only during market hours and see roughly $15M volume on about $100K open interest, showing weak demand for the existing onshore format.
insights.speaker: Tom
insights.so_what: Product design (24/7 perps vs dated futures) matters more than regulatory permission for adoption.
insights.quote: doing like 15 mil volume on like 100k in open interest

themes.theme: Anthropic S-1 and the data-center backlash

insights.claim: After the midterms, Nasdaq rose about 1.8%, Bitcoin about 3% and Ethereum about 6%.
insights.speaker: Haseeb (Dragonfly)
insights.so_what: Risk assets rallied on the election outcome, with ETH outperforming.
insights.quote: Nasdaq was up like 1.8%. Crypto was up Bitcoin was up three Ethereum was up six.

insights.claim: Anthropic's updated S-1 shows Q3 revenue of $17 billion vs $11.5 billion in Q2 (about 50% quarter-over-quarter), a return to a slight operating loss after an operating profit in Q2, and a new risk factor for recursive self-improvement.
insights.speaker: Haseeb (Dragonfly)
insights.so_what: Hypergrowth continues but profitability is not yet stable; RSI now formally disclosed as a risk.
insights.quote: They announced their Q3 revenues, which was 17 billion versus 11 and 1/2 billion they made in Q2.

insights.claim: Anthropic pre-IPO perps rose after the midterms even though many flipped states were data-center states, and data-center ballot propositions were overwhelmingly in one direction (against).
insights.speaker: Haseeb / Tarun
insights.so_what: Political backlash against data centers is broad and is being priced as a supply constraint.

insights.claim: Hedge funds reason that slower new US data-center capacity hurts neoclouds and benefits incumbent hyperscalers and frontier labs that already locked in compute, because it lowers capex burden and blocks new competitors; hyperscalers rose while Nvidia, memory and chip stocks fell.
insights.speaker: Robert (Superstate)
insights.so_what: Trade: long incumbents with locked compute, short neoclouds and chip/memory suppliers on data-center restrictions.
insights.quote: New capacity is going to come online slower than we previously thought, right? This disadvantages Neo Clouds.

insights.claim: Believing that less compute coming online is good for Anthropic implies the market thinks AI is hitting a ceiling on ROI from more compute, which is fundamentally bearish on AI in aggregate even if it boosts incumbents' short- to medium-term earnings.
insights.speaker: Haseeb (Dragonfly)
insights.so_what: The data-center-restriction rally is a bearish signal on long-run AI growth expectations.
insights.quote: the hedge funds are bearish on AI in aggregate in believing that data center's not coming online is good for Anthropic.

insights.claim: Restricting new compute favors whoever already pre-bought it, akin to buying all the chickens so no one can open a new restaurant, entrenching monopoly-style concentration among existing labs.
insights.speaker: Tom / Robert
insights.so_what: Locked compute contracts become a competitive moat under supply restrictions.
insights.quote: It's like they bought all the chickens and so you can't start a new restaurant.

insights.claim: Non-US data-center build-out has accelerated roughly 100x in the past two weeks in capital commitments and foreign debt issuance, and will likely catch up to and perhaps exceed the US; that compute will be sold mostly to neoclouds and consumer apps rather than Anthropic, which prefers US compute.
insights.speaker: Tarun (Gauntlet)
insights.so_what: US restrictions shift AI infrastructure investment offshore, bifurcating into geo-distributed (crypto-like) vs trad hyperscaler compute.
insights.quote: the non-US build-out speed-up is like 100x in the last 2 weeks

insights.claim: Texas, the number one US state for data centers, elected Gina Hinojosa, who ran on a populist anti-tech platform including slowing or possibly a moratorium on new data-center build-outs.
insights.speaker: Haseeb / Robert
insights.so_what: Texas data-center growth assumptions face new state-level political risk.
insights.quote: She explicitly ran on basically slowing down or I think maybe even a moratorium on on new data center build-outs in Texas.

insights.claim: The Foundation for American Innovation published a paper calling 'obliterated' (abliterated, refusal-removed) open-source models a threat and urging regulation and liability for companies that serve them, such as Venice, Near and an abliteration-focused provider.
insights.speaker: Haseeb (Dragonfly)
insights.so_what: A policy push against uncensored open models directly threatens crypto-aligned AI inference businesses (Dragonfly is a Venice investor).

insights.claim: Abliteration cannot be prevented because larger models can easily remove refusals from smaller models, so regulation will never eliminate uncensored models; the better approach is private encrypted inference like Near's.
insights.speaker: Tarun (Gauntlet)
insights.so_what: Uncensored models are a permanent fixture; value accrues to private/verifiable inference infrastructure.
insights.quote: I don't think you're going to ever regulate this type of thing out of existence no matter what Anthropic tells you.

insights.claim: AI will split into unrestricted abliterated models and restricted models (e.g. for formal verification) with separate routers built around them, mirroring how US-regulated validators censor OFAC/Tornado Cash transactions while non-US validators do not.
insights.speaker: Tarun (Gauntlet)
insights.so_what: Expect jurisdiction-segmented inference providers, with US-only guarantees already appearing.
insights.quote: the non-US random validators are running kind of will do anything and you're going to get have the same thing with inference providers.

insights.claim: Frontier lab cyber programs such as OpenAI's Daybreak and Anthropic's Glass Wing still refuse or limit red-teaming, and during the OpenAI Hugging Face attack Hugging Face had to defend itself with an open model because OpenAI refused defensive help.
insights.speaker: Haseeb (Dragonfly)
insights.so_what: Defenders need uncensored models; closed-lab refusals create demand for abliterated inference.
insights.quote: Hugging Face had to defend itself using an open model.

insights.claim: Banning abliterated models is prior restraint, with a straight line from the First and Second Amendments; liability should apply only to negligent hosted inference, since malicious state actors like North Korea self-host while US users of services like Venice are mostly defenders paying with credit cards.
insights.speaker: Haseeb (Dragonfly)
insights.so_what: Legal fight likely to mirror the 1990s crypto export cases; a likely Supreme Court-level question.
insights.quote: I think obliteration is a perfect example of prior restraint.

insights.claim: a16z crypto rebranded as a16z frontier, expanding its mandate beyond crypto to new computing paradigms and agent-to-agent technology, effectively whatever Chris Dixon wants, while still including crypto.
insights.speaker: Haseeb (Dragonfly)
insights.so_what: Signals crypto VC capital drifting toward AI and frontier tech.

insights.claim: When Paradigm announced a crypto-and-AI pivot in 2023 right after ChatGPT, it was bullied into reverting, which in retrospect cost it what would have been an excellent AI vintage; a16z's similar move three years later drew no backlash, a sign of the times.
insights.speaker: Haseeb / Tom
insights.so_what: Crypto community sentiment has shifted to accept AI diversification by crypto funds.
insights.quote: Incredible In retrospect, incredible timing that we bullied them out of.
